B: Black holes: Penrose proved that black holes are a consequence of general relativity, while Genzel and Ghez discovered a supermassive object at the center of the Milky Way.
giai_thich: Penrose used mathematics in 1965 to show that when matter collapses sufficiently, the formation of a black hole is inevitable. Genzel and Ghez, leading two competing teams, tracked the orbits of stars around the center of the Milky Way for over 25 years. The star S2 orbits an invisible object weighing about 4 million times the Sun every 16 years, at speeds reaching around 7,650 km/s. Ghez is the fourth woman to win the Nobel Prize in Physics.

cau_hoi: The 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to Saul Perlmutter, Brian Schmidt, and Adam Riess for what surprising discovery in 1998?
D: The universe is not only expanding but also expanding at an accelerating rate.
giai_thich: Two independent teams observed distant Type Ia supernovae, using them as "standard candles," and found them dimmer than expected, meaning they were farther away. They expected the expansion to slow down due to gravity, but the results were the opposite. The cause was termed "dark energy," which makes up about 68% of the universe, but no one knows what it is yet. Riess recounted that initially, the team thought they had made a calculation error.

cau_hoi: The 2006 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to John Mather and George Smoot for data from the COBE satellite. What did they demonstrate?
A: The Sun is the center of the universe.
C: The cosmic microwave background radiation has a perfect "black body" spectrum and contains tiny temperature fluctuations, the seeds of galaxies.
giai_thich: The measured spectrum matched the theoretical curve so accurately that when presented at a conference in 1990, the audience stood up and applauded. The fluctuations of only about one part in 100,000 showed that the early universe was not completely uniform; slightly denser regions later became galaxies and galaxy clusters. Smoot called that map the "face of God," a statement that sparked controversy. The WMAP and Planck satellites later provided much more detailed measurements.

cau_hoi: In August 2017, the event GW170817, the merger of two neutron stars, was observed by both gravitational waves and light. What important discovery was made?
A: Light travels much slower than gravitational waves.
B: Such collisions produce large amounts of heavy elements like gold and platinum in the "kilonova" explosion.
D: Neutron stars are made of pure gold.
giai_thich: About 1.7 seconds after the gravitational wave signal, satellites recorded a gamma-ray burst, confirming that gravitational waves travel at the speed of light. Around 70 observatories worldwide then pointed their telescopes at the galaxy NGC 4993, about 130 million light-years away. It is estimated that the collision produced gold weighing several to tens of times the mass of Earth. Thus, some gold in wedding rings may come from ancient neutron star collisions.

cau_hoi: In 1992, David Jewitt and Jane Luu discovered the first object (after Pluto and Charon) in which region at the edge of the Solar System?
giai_thich: The object named 15760 Albion, initially designated 1992 QB1. Jewitt and Luu searched for 5 years because they believed the outer edge of the Solar System could not be "empty." The Kuiper Belt is a disk-shaped region containing countless icy bodies beyond Neptune's orbit, the source of many short-period comets. Jane Luu is a Vietnamese-American astronomer, born in Saigon, who moved to the U.S. in 1975. The asteroid 5430 Luu is named after her.

cau_hoi: Dutch astronomer Jan Oort proposed in 1950 that the Solar System is surrounded by what structure?
A: A gigantic spherical cloud containing trillions of icy bodies, the source of long-period comets.
giai_thich: The Oort Cloud could extend up to about 100,000 AU, nearly a quarter to half the distance to the nearest star. Oort noticed that long-period comets come from all directions and from very far away. The gravitational pull of nearby stars or the Milky Way occasionally causes an object from there to fall into the inner Solar System. The Oort Cloud has never been directly observed, as the objects there are too small and too distant.

cau_hoi: In 1950, astronomer Fred Whipple proposed which model for the structure of comets, later confirmed by spacecraft?
D: "Dirty snowball": a chunk of ice mixed with dust and rock.
giai_thich: As comets approach the Sun, ice sublimates into gas, dragging along dust, creating the comet's head and two tails that can be millions of kilometers long. In 1986, the European spacecraft Giotto photographed the nucleus of Halley's comet and found it as dark as coal, much darker than imagined, covered with a layer of carbon-rich dust. The Rosetta mission later showed that comets may resemble "dirty snowballs" more, with more dust than ice.

cau_hoi: In 2015, the Dawn spacecraft discovered mysterious bright spots in the Occator crater on the dwarf planet Ceres. What are they?
D: A layer of sodium carbonate salt, traces of briny water rising from beneath the surface.
giai_thich: Dawn was the first spacecraft to orbit two different celestial bodies beyond Earth: the asteroid Vesta (2011 – 2012) and Ceres (2015 – 2018), thanks to its gentle but persistent ion propulsion system. The bright spots suggest that beneath Ceres' crust, there may still be a reservoir of liquid brine. Ceres is the largest body in the asteroid belt, accounting for about one-third of the total mass of the belt.

cau_hoi: The "cosmic inflation" theory proposed by Alan Guth in 1980 suggests what happened right after the Big Bang?
A: The universe remained static for millions of years.
B: The universe expanded extremely rapidly in a tiny fraction of a second, magnifying by trillions of times.
giai_thich: Inflation explains why the universe appears uniform in all directions even though distant regions have never had time to "exchange" heat, and why space is nearly flat. Tiny quantum fluctuations were magnified into the seeds of galaxies. In his notebook, Guth wrote the phrase "EXTREMELY IMPORTANT INSIGHT" and framed it. Andrei Linde, Alexei Starobinsky, and many others also developed the theory. The exact mechanism has yet to be verified.

cau_hoi: In 2014, the BICEP2 team announced the discovery of traces of "primordial gravitational waves" from the cosmic inflation period. What happened next?
A: Analysis with the Planck satellite data showed that the signal was mainly caused by dust in the Milky Way, so the claim was retracted
D: The claim was immediately awarded the Nobel Prize
giai_thich: The BICEP2 telescope located in Antarctica measured the swirling polarization of the cosmic microwave background radiation. News spread worldwide, with video footage capturing physicist Andrei Linde's emotional reaction upon receiving the news. However, dust in the Milky Way also creates similar polarized signals. In early 2015, joint analysis with the Planck team showed no significant evidence. This incident serves as a lesson about thoroughly checking all sources of noise before making announcements.

cau_hoi: "Hubble tension" is what issue in current cosmology?
B: Two scientists named Hubble are arguing
C: The expansion rate of the universe measured from nearby galaxies (about 73 km/s/Mpc) is higher than that calculated from the cosmic microwave background (about 67 km/s/Mpc)
giai_thich: Two methods, each very accurate, yield results differing by about 8-9%, far exceeding measurement errors. Adam Riess's SH0ES team used Cepheid stars and supernovae, while the Planck team used the cosmic microwave background combined with the standard cosmological model. The James Webb telescope has confirmed that Cepheid star measurements are not confused by crowding. If the tension is real, it may require "new physics," such as dark energy changing over time.

cau_hoi: "Bullet Cluster," studied in 2006, is considered strong evidence for what?
B: The universe has a bullet shape
D: The existence of dark matter, as most of the mass (seen through gravitational lensing) is separated from the hot gas (seen through X-rays)
giai_thich: Two galaxy clusters collided with each other. The hot gas, which makes up most of the ordinary matter, collided and slowed down in the middle, creating shock waves shaped like bullets. However, most of the mass continued to pass through with the galaxies, as if it had not collided with anything. This is difficult to explain if only modifying the laws of gravity, but fits with dark matter, which interacts very little. The map was created using Chandra (X-ray) and Hubble telescopes.

cau_hoi: "Gravitational lensing," predicted by general relativity, creates what phenomenon like the "Einstein Cross"?
A: The telescope broke into a cross shape
B: Light forms a cross due to clouds
C: The gravitational force of a nearby galaxy bends the light of a distant quasar behind it, creating multiple images of the same object
D: Stars randomly align in a cross shape
giai_thich: The Einstein Cross consists of four images of the same quasar located about 8 billion light-years away, arranged around a much closer galaxy. When the distant object, lens, and observer are perfectly aligned, the light forms a circle known as an "Einstein ring." Gravitational lensing acts like a natural magnifying glass, allowing astronomers to see galaxies that are very far away, which would otherwise be too faint.

cau_hoi: In 2014, astronomers identified that the Milky Way belongs to a gigantic galaxy supercluster named what, meaning "vast sky" in Hawaiian?
giai_thich: Laniakea spans about 500 million light-years and contains approximately 100,000 galaxies. R. Brent Tully's research team defined the boundaries by mapping the motion of about 8,000 galaxies, similar to determining the basin of a river: the galaxies in Laniakea all "flow" toward a common gravitational region called the Great Attractor. Our cosmic address: Earth, Solar System, Milky Way, Local Group, Laniakea Supercluster.

cau_hoi: "Boötes Void," discovered in 1981, is what?
A: A vast region of space about 330 million light-years in diameter with almost no galaxies
giai_thich: Normally, such a large region should contain thousands of galaxies, but astronomers have only found about 60 galaxies. Astronomer Greg Aldering humorously remarked that if the Milky Way were in the middle of the Boötes Void, Americans would not have known about other galaxies until the 1960s. The universe has a structure resembling a soap bubble network: galaxies cluster into filaments and walls, interspersed with enormous voids, known as the "cosmic web."

cau_hoi: "Fermi Paradox" arises from the famous question posed by Enrico Fermi during a lunch in 1950. What was that question?
A: "Where is everybody?" — if intelligent life is common in the universe, why have we not seen any signs
giai_thich: The Milky Way has hundreds of billions of stars, many of which are billions of years older than the Sun. If just one civilization knows how to travel through space, they could have spread throughout the galaxy in a few million years. There are many hypotheses: intelligent life is extremely rare; civilizations self-destruct; they are too far away; or they choose not to communicate. The question arose when Fermi and colleagues at Los Alamos were discussing cartoon depictions of flying saucers in the newspaper.

cau_hoi: In 1961, astronomer Frank Drake wrote a famous equation for what purpose?
A: To calculate the age of the universe
B: To estimate the number of civilizations that could communicate via radio waves in the Milky Way
C: To calculate the speed of light
D: To calculate the mass of the Sun
giai_thich: The Drake equation multiplies factors: the rate of star formation, the fraction of stars with planets, the number of planets that could support life, the fraction of planets that develop life, intelligent life, communication technology, and the length of time those civilizations exist. Many factors are completely unknown, so the result can range from nearly 0 to millions. Drake wrote the equation to set the agenda for a meeting at Green Bank, where he conducted Project Ozma, the first search for extraterrestrial signals in 1960.

cau_hoi: "Wow! signal" in 1977 was what?
A: A signal from the Voyager spacecraft
C: A strong, narrow radio signal lasting 72 seconds recorded by the Big Ear telescope (Ohio, USA), never repeated
giai_thich: Astronomer Jerry Ehman circled the string of characters "6EQUJ5" on the computer printout and wrote next to it "Wow!" The signal had a frequency close to 1,420 MHz, the characteristic frequency of hydrogen, which many believe extraterrestrials might choose to communicate. Despite multiple attempts to revisit that region of the sky, no one has seen the signal repeat. In 2024, a study suggested it might have been caused by a hydrogen cloud excited by a strong natural wave source.

cau_hoi: The Arecibo radio telescope (Puerto Rico), once the largest in the world with a diameter of 305 m, had what two famous events?
A: In 1969 welcomed the Apollo spacecraft; in 2000 moved to Europe
B: Discovered Pluto; sold to private owners
C: Captured the first image of a black hole; moved to the Moon
D: In 1974 sent the "Arecibo Message" towards the star cluster M13; in 2020 collapsed due to cable failure
giai_thich: The message consisted of 1,679 bits, depicting numbers, elements of life, DNA, a human figure, the Solar System, and the Arecibo telescope. The number 1,679 is the product of the two prime numbers 23 and 73, allowing the recipient to arrange them into an image. M13 is about 25,000 light-years away. Arecibo also appeared in the James Bond films "GoldenEye" and "Contact." In 2016, China's FAST 500 m telescope in Guizhou surpassed it.

cau_hoi: The world's largest optical telescope under construction, the Extremely Large Telescope (ELT) in Chile, has a primary mirror with a diameter of approximately how much?
B: About 39 m, consisting of 798 hexagonal mirrors
giai_thich: The mirror of the ELT has an area larger than all existing large optical telescopes combined, collecting light approximately 100 million times more than the human eye. The telescope is being built on Cerro Armazones in the Atacama Desert, one of the driest and clearest places on Earth. The ELT will use "adaptive optics," deforming the mirror thousands of times per second to compensate for atmospheric turbulence. An important goal is to study the atmospheres of exoplanets.

cau_hoi: In 2008, what was the famous planetary system around the star HR 8799 known for?
D: One of the first exoplanet systems to be directly imaged, with multiple giant planets
giai_thich: Directly imaging exoplanets is extremely difficult because the star is millions to billions of times brighter than the planet, like trying to see a firefly next to a lighthouse. Astronomers used adaptive optics and techniques to block the star's light at the Keck and Gemini telescopes. Four giant planets, each several times the mass of Jupiter, orbit at a great distance. Astronomers also stitched together years of images into a movie showing the planets moving in orbit.

cau_hoi: In 2011, the Kepler telescope discovered the planet Kepler-16b, referred to by the media as the "real Tatooine" from the Star Wars movie. Why?
A: It orbits two stars at once, so it could have two suns rising and setting
giai_thich: Kepler-16b is a Saturn-sized planet that orbits a pair of stars, a orange dwarf and a red dwarf, that orbit each other. This is the first confirmed "circumbinary planet" using the transit method. The planet is quite cold and likely has no life. About half of Sun-like stars have companions, so such planets may be quite common.

cau_hoi: The exoplanet HD 189733b is famous for what strange weather conditions?
C: Deep blue color, extreme winds, and possibly "glass rain" blowing sideways
giai_thich: The planet is a "hot Jupiter" located about 64 light-years away, with temperatures around 1,000°C. In 2013, the Hubble telescope measured its blue color, possibly due to silicate particles in the atmosphere scattering light. Winds can reach about 8,700 km/h, approximately 7 times the speed of sound on Earth. In 2024, the James Webb telescope also detected hydrogen sulfide there, meaning the planet could smell like rotten eggs.

cau_hoi: In 2025, a research team reported the possibility of DMS molecules, a substance on Earth primarily produced by marine organisms, in the atmosphere of the planet K2-18b. How did the scientific community react?
B: Skeptical: independent analyses showed the signal was weak and not certain enough to conclude
D: Sent a spacecraft to the planet immediately
giai_thich: K2-18b is about 124 light-years away and weighs about 8.6 times that of Earth. Nikku Madhusudhan's team suggested it could be a "Hycean" planet, with an ocean of water beneath a hydrogen-rich atmosphere. The James Webb telescope has clearly detected methane and CO₂. However, many scientists pointed out that the DMS signal could be due to data processing, and the planet could also be a gas giant without a water surface. Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence.

cau_hoi: In 1844, Friedrich Bessel predicted that the star Sirius had an invisible companion. What type of star was that companion, Sirius B, discovered in 1862?
D: White dwarf, the first known white dwarf
giai_thich: Bessel observed Sirius wobbling slightly in the sky as if being pulled by an invisible heavy object. Telescope maker Alvan Graham Clark saw Sirius B while testing a new lens in 1862. Sirius B has a mass nearly equal to that of the Sun but is only about the size of Earth, so a spoonful of its material weighs several tons. Sirius is the brightest star in the night sky, located about 8.6 light-years away. Ancient Egyptians relied on the timing of Sirius rising before dawn to predict the flooding season of the Nile.

cau_hoi: In 1838, how did Friedrich Bessel first measure the distance to a star (61 Cygni)?
A: Parallax: measuring the very small shift in the star's position when Earth is on opposite sides of its orbit
giai_thich: Similar to looking at a finger alternately with the left and right eye, the finger appears to shift against the distant background. For stars, the angle of shift is extremely small, only about 0.3 arc seconds, equivalent to the size of a coin viewed from about 10 km away. Bessel calculated the distance to be about 10 light-years, close to the correct value of 11.4 light-years. The inability to measure parallax previously was used as an argument against the heliocentric theory.

cau_hoi: What is the significance of the "Hertzsprung – Russell diagram," created around 1910 – 1913, for astronomers?
B: A map of the positions of stars
C: Arranging stars by brightness and temperature, showing that most stars lie on a "main sequence," helping to understand stellar evolution
giai_thich: Ejnar Hertzsprung (Denmark) and Henry Norris Russell (USA) independently created this diagram. About 90% of stars, including the Sun, lie on the main sequence, where they burn hydrogen in their cores. Red giant stars are located at the upper right corner: cool but very bright due to their size. White dwarfs are at the lower left corner: hot but dim due to their small size. The position of a star on the diagram changes as it ages.

cau_hoi: Who coined the term "Big Bang" in 1949, a person who actually supported an opposing theory?
A: Fred Hoyle, an astronomer who supported the "steady state" theory that the universe has no beginning
giai_thich: Hoyle used the phrase in a BBC radio program. Many think he used it mockingly, although he said he just wanted to create an understandable image for listeners. The steady state theory posits that new matter is continuously created as the universe expands. The discovery of cosmic microwave background radiation in 1965 led most scientists to abandon this theory, but Hoyle continued to reject the Big Bang until the end of his life. In fact, it was not an "explosion" in space but the expansion of space itself.

cau_hoi: Under what circumstances did Karl Schwarzschild find the first exact solution to Einstein's equations, describing spacetime around a sphere, in 1915?
C: While serving in the German army on the Eastern Front during World War I
giai_thich: Schwarzschild sent the results to Einstein, who was surprised because he did not think it was possible to find an exact solution so quickly. The solution contains the "Schwarzschild radius": if an object is compressed smaller than this radius, it becomes a black hole. For Earth, this radius is only about 9 mm, the size of a marble; for the Sun, about 3 km. Schwarzschild died in 1916 from an illness contracted at the front, just a few months after this discovery.

cau_hoi: In 1783, English pastor and scientist John Michell proposed what idea, considered a precursor to the concept of black holes?
D: "Dark stars": a star massive and dense enough that light cannot escape its gravitational pull
giai_thich: Based on Newton's particle theory of light, Michell calculated that if a star had the same density as the Sun but a radius about 500 times larger, the escape velocity would exceed the speed of light. He also suggested that these invisible stars could be detected by their gravitational influence on nearby stars, which is indeed how astronomers detect black holes today. Pierre-Simon Laplace had a similar idea in 1796.

cau_hoi: In 1974, Stephen Hawking bet Kip Thorne that Cygnus X-1 was not a black hole. What was the outcome?
B: Hawking lost the bet in 1990 when evidence showed it was indeed a black hole, and had to give Thorne a year's subscription to a magazine
giai_thich: Cygnus X-1 is a strong X-ray source in the constellation Cygnus, consisting of a blue supergiant star and an unseen object weighing about 20 times the Sun. Hawking explained he made the bet as a "insurance policy": if black holes did not exist, many years of his work would be wasted, but at least he would receive a prize. Cygnus X-1 was one of the first objects widely accepted as a black hole.

cau_hoi: Christiaan Huygens made two major discoveries about Saturn between 1655 and 1659. What were they?
B: Discovered Saturn's largest moon (Titan) and correctly explained that Saturn has a thin flat ring surrounding it
giai_thich: Galileo had seen Saturn with two strange "ears" that then disappeared, as at that time the rings were edge-on to Earth. Huygens used a better telescope and published his solution in the form of a riddle to maintain priority. He also invented the pendulum clock. The Huygens lander that landed on Titan in 2005 was named after him. Titan is the only moon in the Solar System with a thick atmosphere.

cau_hoi: In 1675, astronomer Giovanni Domenico Cassini discovered what on Saturn, now named after him?
D: A wide dark gap between Saturn's two main rings (Cassini Division)
giai_thich: The Cassini Division is about 4,800 km wide, longer than the length of Vietnam, and is not completely empty but contains fewer particles. The gap formed due to the gravitational pull of the moon Mimas "clearing" out particles in an orbit with a period exactly half that of Mimas, known as orbital resonance. Cassini also discovered four moons of Saturn, including Iapetus, which has one half bright and the other half dark. NASA and ESA's Cassini spacecraft is named after him.

cau_hoi: In 1729, English astronomer James Bradley discovered "stellar aberration", the first direct evidence for what?
A: The Earth moves around the Sun
giai_thich: Bradley was trying to measure the parallax of Gamma Draconis when he noticed it moved in a way that did not resemble parallax. According to legend, he came up with the solution while boating on the Thames and saw the flag on the mast change direction as the boat changed direction, even though the wind remained constant. Just like when running in the rain, one must tilt the umbrella forward; the telescope must be tilted slightly in the direction of the Earth's motion. From this, he calculated the speed of light more accurately than Rømer.

cau_hoi: What achievement did English astronomer Thomas Harriot have related to the Moon, a few months earlier than Galileo?
A: First to set foot on the Moon
B: Measured the distance to the Moon using lasers
C: Drew the first known map of the Moon through a telescope on July 26, 1609
giai_thich: Harriot used a telescope that magnified about 6 times and sketched the Moon with its light-dark boundary. However, he did not publish, so Galileo, who published "Sidereus Nuncius" in 1610 with detailed drawings of the Moon's mountains and craters, became more widely known. Harriot also observed sunspots and Jupiter's moons. He participated in Walter Raleigh's expedition to America.

cau_hoi: In 1995, how did the Hubble telescope take the "Hubble Deep Field" image and what was the surprising result?
A: Pointed at a seemingly empty area of the sky, as small as a grain of sand held at arm's length, for about 10 days, and saw about 3,000 galaxies
B: Took a picture of Earth from afar
C: Took a picture of the Sun over 1 year
D: Took a picture of the Moon in 1 second
giai_thich: Robert Williams, director of the Space Telescope Science Institute, decided to use his own observing time, even though many thought it was a waste as nothing might be seen. The image showed that almost every bright dot was a galaxy, many galaxies very far away. If multiplied across the entire sky, the universe contains hundreds of billions of galaxies. Subsequent versions like the Ultra Deep Field (2004) and Extreme Deep Field (2012) looked even further.

cau_hoi: In 1612 – 1613, Galileo debated with priest Christoph Scheiner about what?
B: The nature of sunspots: Galileo argued they were on the surface of the Sun, while Scheiner claimed they were small satellites orbiting it
giai_thich: At that time, many believed the Sun was a perfect celestial body, without blemish. Galileo observed the spots moving, changing shape, and shrinking as they approached the edge of the Sun's disk, proving they were on the surface of a rotating Sun. Galileo projected the Sun's image onto paper instead of looking directly, a safe method devised by his student Benedetto Castelli. Later, Scheiner agreed that the spots were on the Sun and wrote a large book about them.

cau_hoi: In 1859, Urbain Le Verrier discovered that Mercury's orbit deviated slightly from Newton's calculations and guessed there was a mysterious planet near the Sun. What did he call it, and what was the actual explanation?
C: "Vulcan"; actually explained by Einstein's general relativity in 1915
giai_thich: The point closest to the Sun in Mercury's orbit gradually shifts, deviating about 43 arc seconds per century from predictions. After successfully predicting Neptune, Le Verrier believed there was another hidden planet. Many even claimed to have seen Vulcan passing in front of the Sun. In 1915, Einstein calculated the exact 43 arc seconds from general relativity and recounted that he was so excited his heart raced. Vulcan does not exist.

cau_hoi: At the end of the 19th century, Percival Lowell built an observatory in Arizona and became famous for what mistaken belief about Mars?
D: Mars has a system of "canals" built by a civilization to channel water from the poles
giai_thich: In 1877, Italian astronomer Giovanni Schiaparelli drew thin lines on Mars and called them "canali", meaning channels, but it was translated into English as "canals". Lowell drew hundreds of canals and wrote famous books, inspiring H. G. Wells' novel "The War of the Worlds". In 1965, the Mariner 4 spacecraft took close-up images showing no canals, only impact craters. It was an illusion caused by the eye connecting blurry spots into lines.

cau_hoi: In 1918, astronomer Harlow Shapley used globular clusters to prove what about the Sun's position?
A: The Sun is the center of the universe
B: The Sun is not at the center of the Milky Way but is quite far, near the edge of the galactic disk
C: The Sun is at the center of the Milky Way
D: The Sun is outside the Milky Way
giai_thich: Shapley observed that globular clusters, each containing hundreds of thousands of stars, are not evenly distributed across the sky but are concentrated towards the Sagittarius constellation. He believed they surrounded the center of the Milky Way, so the center must be in that direction. Today we know the Sun is about 26,000 light-years from the center of the Milky Way and takes about 230 million years to orbit the center, known as a "galactic year." The last time the Sun was in its current position, the first dinosaurs had just appeared.

cau_hoi: In 2022, the Hubble telescope discovered "Earendel." What record does this object hold?
A: The farthest single star ever observed, emitting light when the universe was less than 1 billion years old
giai_thich: Normally, a single star cannot be seen at that distance, but Earendel is positioned in a spot magnified thousands of times by the gravitational lensing of a foreground galaxy cluster. Its light has traveled about 12.9 billion years. The name Earendel means "morning star" in Old English and is also the name of a character in J. R. R. Tolkien's stories. The star may weigh at least 50 times that of the Sun. The James Webb telescope later observed and confirmed it.

cau_hoi: In 2024, the James Webb telescope confirmed that the galaxy JADES-GS-z14-0 is the farthest known galaxy at that time. When did its light emit when the universe was approximately how old?
giai_thich: The galaxy has a redshift of about 14.3. Surprisingly, it is quite bright and large, spanning about 1,600 light-years, and shows signs of containing oxygen, meaning generations of stars had time to live and die in a very short period. In 2025, another galaxy, MoM-z14, was announced to be even farther away. Many early galaxies discovered by James Webb are brighter and more numerous than expected, forcing scientists to reconsider galaxy formation models.

cau_hoi: "Population III stars" are what, and why are astronomers searching for them?
B: Stars that only exist on the Moon
C: The first stars in the universe, almost entirely composed of hydrogen and helium, likely very massive; they created the first heavy elements
giai_thich: After the Big Bang, the universe only contained hydrogen, helium, and a little lithium. All heavier elements, such as carbon, oxygen, and iron in our bodies, were created in the cores of stars. Astronomers refer to them in reverse order: Population I stars like the Sun are young and metal-rich, Population II stars are older and metal-poor, and Population III stars are the first generation. To date, no Population III stars have been definitively confirmed, although James Webb has seen some potential signs.

cau_hoi: The star Eta Carinae attracted attention in the 19th century for what event?
D: "The Great Eruption" of the 1840s, when it temporarily became the second brightest star in the sky and expelled two massive clouds
giai_thich: Eta Carinae is an extremely massive binary star system, located about 7,500 light-years away, with the primary star weighing approximately 90 – 100 times that of the Sun. During the eruption, it expelled a mass equivalent to about 10 Suns, forming the Homunculus nebula ("little man") shaped like two balloons. The star may explode into a supernova or hypernova in the near future on the astronomical scale. It can only be seen in the southern sky.

cau_hoi: R136a1, a star in the Tarantula Nebula (Large Magellanic Cloud), holds what record?
A: The heaviest known star, about 200 times the mass of the Sun according to recent estimates
giai_thich: When announced in 2010, its estimated mass was about 265 – 315 times that of the Sun; sharper observations in 2022 reduced it to about 170 – 230 times. It is millions of times brighter than the Sun and has a temperature of about 46,000 K. Such massive stars have very short lifespans, only a few million years, and lose mass quickly through extremely strong stellar winds. If R136a1 replaced the Sun, it would shine brighter than the Sun does compared to the full Moon.

cau_hoi: The red supergiant star Stephenson 2-18 is famous for what?
B: Being one of the largest known stars, with a radius possibly about 2,000 times that of the Sun
giai_thich: If placed in the Sun's position, its surface could extend beyond the orbit of Saturn. Light takes about 9 hours to circle the star's surface, while it takes only about 14.5 seconds to circle the Sun. However, the sizes of red supergiant stars are very difficult to measure due to unclear surfaces and uncertain distances, so the numbers may vary. Despite being so large, it is not the heaviest, as its outer layer is very diffuse.

cau_hoi: The star KIC 8462852, known as "Tabby's Star," caused a stir in 2015 for what phenomenon?
C: Unusually and unevenly dimming by about 22%, leading some to speculate about "alien structures"
giai_thich: Astronomer Tabetha Boyajian discovered the phenomenon thanks to volunteers in the Planet Hunters project, who were reviewing Kepler data. Some proposed the idea of a "Dyson sphere," a massive structure built by an advanced civilization to harvest stellar energy. Subsequent observations showed that the dimming was stronger in blue light, consistent with dust rather than solid objects. This is an example of how science carefully considers strange hypotheses.

cau_hoi: The star HD 140283, nicknamed "Methuselah Star," once puzzled astronomers for what reason?
A: It is the youngest star in the universe
D: Its initial age estimate seems to exceed the age of the universe, although the margin of error allows both values to be consistent
giai_thich: In 2013, the estimated age of the star was about 14.5 billion years with an error margin of about 0.8 billion years, while the age of the universe is about 13.8 billion years. Subsequent estimates were lowered to about 12 – 13 billion years, which is more consistent. The star contains very little metal, meaning it formed from gas that had not been significantly "enriched" by previous generations of stars. It is about 200 light-years away and is one of the oldest stars with a fairly accurate age measurement. Methuselah is the longest-lived character in the Bible.

cau_hoi: On December 27, 2004, a magnetar named SGR 1806-20, located about 50,000 light-years away, emitted a massive gamma-ray burst. What happened?
A: The radiation was so strong that it temporarily altered the ionosphere of the Earth, even though the source was on the other side of the Milky Way
D: The Earth was pushed off its orbit
giai_thich: In about 0.2 seconds, the magnetar released more energy than the Sun emits in about 100,000 years. Magnetars are neutron stars with the strongest magnetic fields in the universe, millions of trillions of times stronger than Earth's. At a distance of 1,000 km, that magnetic field could erase data on all credit cards on Earth; closer, it could distort atoms in the body. The gamma-ray burst was likely caused by a "starquake" that cracked the star's shell.

cau_hoi: The white dwarf star BPM 37093, located about 50 light-years away, was nicknamed by astronomers after which song by The Beatles?
B: "Lucy", because its core has likely crystallized into a giant carbon "diamond"
giai_thich: The name comes from the song "Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds". As the white dwarf cools, carbon and oxygen in its core solidify into crystals, resembling diamonds but at extremely high pressure. Small oscillations of the star allow astronomers to "listen" inside it, similar to how seismologists study the Earth's interior. In about 5 billion years, the Sun will also become a white dwarf and may crystallize. In 2019, the Gaia telescope provided evidence of crystallization in many white dwarfs.

cau_hoi: In 1995, astronomers confirmed Gliese 229B as the first clearly observed "brown dwarf". What is a brown dwarf?
C: An object larger than a planet but not massive enough to sustain hydrogen fusion like a true star, sometimes called a "failed star"
giai_thich: Brown dwarfs typically weigh about 13 – 80 times that of Jupiter, emitting weak light primarily in the infrared spectrum. Gliese 229B has methane in its atmosphere similar to Jupiter, located about 19 light-years away. In 2024, astronomers unexpectedly discovered that Gliese 229B is actually a pair of two brown dwarfs orbiting each other every 12 days, explaining why it appeared unusually heavy. The temperatures of some of the coldest brown dwarfs are close to room temperature.

cau_hoi: The star Algol in the constellation Perseus, known as "the demon's head" by Arabs, is famous for what?
A: Its brightness decreases significantly about every 2.87 days, as it is a binary star system that eclipses each other
giai_thich: In 1783, the 18-year-old deaf Englishman John Goodricke accurately measured the period of variability and proposed that a dimmer star passes in front of the brighter star. He was awarded the prestigious Copley Medal. Goodricke died at the age of 21. The name Algol comes from the Arabic "ra's al-ghūl", and in Greek mythology, the star symbolizes the head of the monster Medusa in the hands of the hero Perseus.

cau_hoi: Barnard's star, a red dwarf about 6 light-years away, holds what record in the sky?
D: The fastest proper motion, moving across the sky a distance equal to the Moon's diameter in about 180 years
giai_thich: Edward Emerson Barnard discovered this in 1916. Because it is close and moves quickly through space, it "runs" across the sky faster than any other star. This is the closest single star to the Sun and the second closest after the Alpha Centauri system. For decades, claims of planets around Barnard's star went unconfirmed, but in 2024 – 2025, astronomers announced the discovery of four small planets orbiting very close to it, too hot for life.

cau_hoi: In 1938, Hans Bethe explained the energy source of stars. He received the Nobel Prize in 1967 for describing which reaction chains?
B: The proton-proton chain and the CNO cycle, converting hydrogen into helium
giai_thich: The Sun primarily uses the proton-proton chain. Heavier and hotter stars mainly use the CNO cycle, in which carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen act as catalysts. Every second, the Sun converts about 600 million tons of hydrogen into helium, and about 4 million tons of mass is converted into energy according to E = mc². According to legend, after coming up with the solution, Bethe took a walk with his girlfriend, and when she praised the beauty of the stars, he said: "And I am the only person in the world who knows why they shine."

cau_hoi: The famous 1957 paper "B²FH" by Burbidge, Burbidge, Fowler, and Hoyle explains what?
C: How chemical elements from carbon to uranium are created in the cores of stars and in supernova explosions
giai_thich: The paper, over 100 pages long, describes many processes: fusion in stellar cores, the "slow neutron capture" process in giant stars, and "rapid neutron capture" in extreme events. Carl Sagan's famous quote, "we are made of star stuff", is based on this work. Margaret Burbidge later became the first female director of the Royal Greenwich Observatory. Fowler received the Nobel Prize in 1983, while Hoyle did not, which many consider unfair.

cau_hoi: In 1953, Fred Hoyle predicted that the carbon-12 nucleus must have a special energy state (about 7.65 MeV). Why is this prediction famous?
A: Because without that state, stars could not produce enough carbon, and life as we know it would not exist; subsequent experiments confirmed this
C: Because it proves the Sun is made of carbon
giai_thich: In stars, three helium nuclei must combine to form carbon, but the probability is too small unless there is a "resonance" at the right energy level. Hoyle argued in reverse: since we exist and our bodies contain carbon, that state must exist. He convinced William Fowler's group at Caltech to conduct experiments, and they found it. This is often referred to as an example of the "anthropic argument" in science, although it remains controversial.

cau_hoi: In a 1948 paper on the origin of light elements after the Big Bang, Ralph Alpher and George Gamow humorously added Hans Bethe as an author for what reason?
B: Because Bethe discovered the Big Bang
C: Because Bethe wrote the entire paper
D: To make the authors' names resemble the first three letters of the Greek alphabet: Alpher, Bethe, Gamow (alpha, beta, gamma)
giai_thich: Gamow was famously humorous. The paper was published in the Physical Review journal on April 1, April Fool's Day. Alpher, then a graduate student who did most of the work, worried that the prominent names of Gamow and Bethe would overshadow his contribution. In the same year, Alpher and Robert Herman predicted that the universe today must have residual radiation with a temperature of about 5 K, close to the 2.7 K measured in 1965. The theory correctly explained the ratio of about 25% helium in the universe.

cau_hoi: In 2003, astronomers discovered Sedna, a distant object with a strange orbit. What makes Sedna special?
C: An extremely long elliptical orbit, taking about 11,000 years to complete one around the Sun, and never coming close to Neptune
giai_thich: At its closest point, Sedna is about 76 AU from the Sun, while at its farthest point, it is about 900 – 1,000 AU. Because it never comes close enough to be influenced by Neptune, scientists wonder what pushed it into that orbit: possibly a star passing by when the Sun was still in the star cluster where it was born, or an undiscovered planet. The name is derived from the Inuit goddess of the sea. Sedna is red, one of the reddest objects in the Solar System.

cau_hoi: In 2019, the New Horizons spacecraft flew past Arrokoth, the farthest object ever visited by a spacecraft. What shape does Arrokoth have?
B: Two flat lobes stuck together like a flattened snowman
giai_thich: Arrokoth is about 6.6 billion km from the Sun, approximately 36 km long. The two lobes appear to have approached and "kissed" gently at a speed of only a few km/h, without crashing into each other. This supports the idea that small planets form from gently collapsing dust clouds. The object is red due to organic compounds. The name Arrokoth means "sky" in the language of the Powhatan people in the Chesapeake region (USA), where the mission control center is located.

cau_hoi: In 2023, astronomers discovered that the dwarf planet Quaoar has what that "breaks the rules"?
A: It has a ring located beyond the Roche limit, where theory suggests that material should coalesce into a moon.
B: It has a sea of water.
giai_thich: According to theory, material closer to a celestial body than the "Roche limit" will be torn apart by tidal forces into a ring, while farther out it will coalesce into a moon. Quaoar's ring is located about 7 times the radius of the celestial body, much farther than this limit. The discovery was made through the phenomenon of occultation, when Quaoar passed in front of a star and the star's light flickered before and after being obscured by Quaoar. The dwarf planet Haumea (2017) and the asteroid Chariklo (2013) also have rings.

cau_hoi: In 2013, astronomers unexpectedly discovered which celestial body is the first small object (not a planet) known to have a ring system?
D: Chariklo, a centaur orbiting the Sun between Saturn and Uranus
giai_thich: Chariklo is only about 250 km wide but has two thin rings, discovered when it occulted a star and astronomers in South America saw the star's light blocked twice before and after the main body. The two rings are named after two rivers in Brazil: Oiapoque and Chuí. Centaurs are celestial bodies that have characteristics of both asteroids and comets, similar to the half-human, half-horse creatures in mythology. The origin of its rings is still unclear.

cau_hoi: In March 2025, astronomers announced the discovery of 128 new moons of Saturn. After that, how many moons does Saturn have in total that are recognized?
giai_thich: Most are small moons just a few kilometers wide, with inclined and distant orbits, likely remnants of collisions. Edward Ashton's team used the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope and "stacking" techniques to detect these faint objects. Saturn now has more moons than all other planets combined. One scientist joked that perhaps such small objects should be called "mini-moons" or "debris." Jupiter has about 95 recognized moons.

cau_hoi: In 2020, a group of scientists announced the discovery of phosphine gas in the clouds of Venus, which could be a sign of life. What happened afterward?
B: It sparked major controversy: many analyses suggested the signal was much weaker or could be due to other gases, and the question remains unresolved.
giai_thich: On Earth, phosphine is primarily produced by microorganisms living in oxygen-poor environments. Jane Greaves' team used the JCMT and ALMA telescopes. Later, they discovered a data processing error in ALMA that significantly reduced the signal. Some studies suggested it could be sulfur dioxide. The cloud layer at an altitude of about 50 – 60 km has temperatures and pressures similar to Earth, but is very acidic. The incident prompted new missions to Venus such as NASA's DAVINCI and VERITAS.

cau_hoi: NASA's InSight lander (2018 – 2022) recorded what for the first time on Mars?
D: Marsquakes, over 1,300 events, helping to study the planet's internal structure.
giai_thich: InSight's SEIS seismometer is sensitive enough to detect vibrations smaller than the size of a hydrogen atom. The strongest quake, about 4.7 magnitude, was recorded in May 2022. Thanks to seismic waves, scientists measured Mars' liquid core, with a radius of about 1,800 km, larger than expected. InSight also "heard" meteoroids hitting Mars. In 2024, InSight data suggested there might be liquid water at depths of about 11 – 20 km in fractured rock. The lander ceased operations when dust covered its solar panels.

cau_hoi: In 1985, the Lunar New Year in Vietnam and China fell on two different days. Why?
C: Vietnam uses UTC+7 time zone, while China uses UTC+8, so the new moon timing fell on two different days in the two countries.
D: China skipped the New Year that year.
giai_thich: The Vietnamese lunar calendar is actually a lunisolar calendar: the first day is the day of the new moon (sóc). In 1967, Northern Vietnam officially switched to calculating time according to Hanoi time zone (UTC+7). In 1985, the new moon occurred around 11:30 PM on January 20 according to Vietnamese time, but at 12:30 AM on January 21 according to Beijing time. Therefore, the New Year in Vietnam was January 20, one day earlier than China, and the previous December in Vietnam only had 29 days. The Vietnamese calendar was calculated by astronomers at the Institute of Physics.

cau_hoi: "The Hunt for Planet Nine" began in 2016 when Konstantin Batygin and Mike Brown presented what evidence?
A: The orbits of some distant objects in the Kuiper Belt are "clumped" unusually, as if being pulled by an undiscovered large planet.
D: Saw a new planet with the naked eye.
giai_thich: According to calculations, Planet Nine could weigh about 5 – 10 times that of Earth, orbiting at a distance of several hundred AU, taking about 10,000 – 20,000 years to complete one orbit. At such a distance, it is extremely faint. Some scientists believe the clumping is merely due to data selection methods during observations. The Vera C. Rubin Observatory may help find it or rule out the hypothesis. Mike Brown is known for discovering Eris, which contributed to Pluto being "demoted," earning him the nickname "the man who killed Pluto."

cau_hoi: In the 1970s, which Indian-American astronomer discovered the first 14 moons in total... — please replace this question with: The Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile announced its first images in June 2025. What is its notable feature?
B: The world's largest digital camera, about 3,200 megapixels, capturing the entire southern sky several nights a week for 10 years.
D: The smallest telescope in the world.
giai_thich: The LSST camera is the size of a small car. Each image is detailed enough that it would take hundreds of ultra-high-definition TV screens to display it fully. Each night, the observatory collects about 20 terabytes of data. The "Legacy Survey of Space and Time" project will create a "movie" of the universe, discovering millions of asteroids, supernovae, and transient objects. In just a few hours of the first test observations, the observatory discovered over 2,000 new asteroids.

cau_hoi: Comet C/2023 A3 (Tsuchinshan – ATLAS) made an impression in October 2024 for what reason?
C: Brightly lit, visible to the naked eye, with the rare phenomenon of a "reverse tail" pointing towards the Sun.
giai_thich: The comet was discovered in 2023 by the Zijiang Observatory (China) and the ATLAS system in South Africa. Many worried it would disintegrate as it approached the Sun, but it survived. The "reverse tail" is actually an illusion due to the observation position: Earth passes through the comet's orbital plane, so we see large dust particles behind the comet appearing to point forward. In Vietnam, many people photographed the comet in the western sky at twilight.

chu_de: "Baryon Acoustic Oscillations" (BAO), discovered in 2005 through galaxy maps, are used by cosmologists for what?
D: As a "standard ruler" about 500 million light-years imprinted in the distribution of galaxies, helping to measure the history of the universe's expansion.
giai_thich: In the early universe, sound waves propagated through a hot "soup" of plasma. As the universe cooled and the waves "froze," they left behind a preferred distance between regions of matter. Today, galaxies tend to be spaced apart by that distance a bit more. In 2024 – 2025, the DESI project with 5,000 fiber optics will measure tens of millions of galaxies and suggest that dark energy may be weakening over time, a result that could change cosmology if confirmed.

cau_hoi: What does the "Grand Tack" model propose happened to Jupiter when the Solar System was newly formed?
B: Jupiter drifted close to the Sun to about the current orbit of Mars, then was pulled back out by Saturn, explaining why Mars is small
giai_thich: The name comes from the sailing term "tack", meaning to change direction against the wind. As Jupiter moved in, its gravitational force "cleared" material in the Mars region, leaving Mars with little material to grow, making it only about 11% the mass of Earth. The model also explains why the asteroid belt consists of two types: dry asteroids on the inside and water-rich, carbonaceous asteroids on the outside. This remains a hypothesis, along with the "Nice model" regarding the movement of giant planets.

cau_hoi: In 2023, NASA launched the Psyche spacecraft to asteroid 16 Psyche. Why is this asteroid special?
A: It may be the exposed metallic core of a primordial planet that lost its rocky outer layer due to a collision
giai_thich: Psyche is about 220 km wide and appears to contain a lot of iron and nickel. Studying it helps understand Earth's core, which humans cannot reach. The press once stated Psyche is "worth 10 quintillion dollars" if all the metals were extracted, but that is just a fun number as it cannot be brought back and would crash metal prices. The spacecraft uses a xenon gas electric propulsion system and is expected to arrive in 2029. Psyche is named after a princess in Greek mythology, the wife of the god Eros.

cau_hoi: In November 2023, NASA's Lucy spacecraft flew past the small asteroid Dinkinesh and discovered what surprising thing?
B: Dinkinesh has a small moon, and that moon is actually two bodies stuck together
giai_thich: The moon is named Selam, meaning "peace" in Amharic. The name Dinkinesh, meaning "you are truly wonderful", is the Ethiopian name for the fossilized skeleton Lucy. The Lucy spacecraft is named after this fossil because the Trojan asteroids it will study are likened to the "fossils" of the planet formation period. The Trojan asteroids accompany Jupiter's orbit, located about 60° ahead and behind the planet. The spacecraft carries a plaque inscribed with quotes from many scientists and artists.

cau_hoi: In 2008, NASA's Phoenix lander near the northern pole of Mars confirmed what when it dug into the surface soil?
A: There is water ice just below the surface; the white chunks in the trench evaporated after a few days
giai_thich: The white chunks, about the size of dice, disappeared in about four days, proving they were water ice sublimating, not salt. Phoenix also detected perchlorate in the soil, a type of salt that could be both an energy source for microorganisms and toxic. The spacecraft also observed snow falling from clouds but evaporating before reaching the ground. Phoenix operated for about 5 months before ceasing when the Martian winter arrived and CO₂ ice covered it.

cau_hoi: In 2015, the Hubble telescope provided evidence of a subsurface salty ocean beneath the surface of Ganymede by observing what phenomenon?
C: Seeing ocean waves on the surface
D: The "wobble" of auroras on Ganymede is less than expected, due to the salty ocean conducting electricity against Jupiter's magnetic field
giai_thich: Ganymede is the only moon in the Solar System with its own magnetic field, so it has auroras. As Jupiter rotates, its magnetic field changes, causing Ganymede's auroras to shift. If there is a layer of salty water that conducts electricity, it creates a secondary magnetic field that counteracts, causing the auroras to shift only about 2° instead of 6°. The ocean could be about 100 km deep, lying beneath a thick layer of ice about 150 km, containing more water than all of Earth's oceans. The JUICE spacecraft is expected to arrive at Ganymede in the early 2030s.

cau_hoi: NASA's Dragonfly mission, scheduled for launch in 2028, will send what type of vehicle to Titan's surface?
C: An eight-rotor drone powered by nuclear energy, flying from one point to another
giai_thich: Titan has an atmosphere about 1.5 times thicker than Earth's and gravity only about one-seventh, making flying there much easier than on Earth. It is jokingly said that on Titan, humans could wear wings and flap to fly. Dragonfly will study organic chemistry on the surface, like natural "laboratories" for prebiotic molecules. The spacecraft is expected to reach Titan around 2034, after about 6 years of flight.

cau_hoi: The Verona Rupes cliff on Miranda, a moon of Uranus, holds what record?
B: Possibly the highest cliff in the Solar System, about 20 km high
giai_thich: The cliff is nearly twice the height of Everest from the base, captured by the Voyager 2 spacecraft in 1986. Due to Miranda's very weak gravity, if someone fell from the top, they would take about 12 minutes to reach the bottom, enough time to enjoy the view while falling, and land at a speed of about 200 km/h. Miranda has a chaotic surface that looks like it is made from many pieces, possibly having been shattered and reassembled or deformed by tidal forces.

cau_hoi: The dark red region at the northern pole of Charon, Pluto's largest moon, was nicknamed "Mordor" by New Horizons scientists. Where does this red color come from?
A: Methane gas escaping from Pluto's atmosphere is trapped by Charon in the cold polar region, then transformed by light into red organic compounds
giai_thich: Charon is about half the size of Pluto, so the two bodies are often considered a "double dwarf planet", orbiting around a point outside both. They are tidally locked to each other: always showing the same face to each other. Mordor is the name of a dark land in "The Lord of the Rings". The red compound is collectively known as "tholin", which also colors the surface of Pluto and Arrokoth.

cau_hoi: Comet ISON was dubbed the "comet of the century" by the press in 2013. What happened to it?
C: It shone as bright as the Sun for a year
D: It disintegrated when flying close to the Sun on Thanksgiving in the US (November 28, 2013)
giai_thich: ISON is a "sungrazing comet", passing within about 1.2 million km of the Sun's surface. The extreme heat and strong tidal forces tore it apart. After passing, a faint bright spot appeared, leading many to hope it survived, but the remnants eventually faded. The event showed that predicting a comet's brightness is very difficult. Astronomer David Levy famously said: "Comets are like cats: they have tails, and they do exactly what they want."

cau_hoi: In 1996, NASA scientists announced that the meteorite ALH84001 from Mars, found in Antarctica in 1984, might contain what?
C: Traces that could be microfossils of bacteria, a highly controversial claim that most scientists now consider to be of abiotic origin
giai_thich: The meteorite was ejected from Mars due to a collision about 17 million years ago and fell to Earth about 13,000 years ago. US President Bill Clinton even spoke on television about this discovery. The structures are smaller than most bacteria on Earth, and the magnetic minerals could form without biological activity. Nevertheless, the event significantly boosted the field of astrobiology and missions to find life on Mars.

cau_hoi: In 2020, scientists determined that some dust particles in the Murchison meteorite (which fell in Australia in 1969) are approximately how old, older than the Solar System?
C: Up to about 7 billion years, this is the oldest solid material ever found on Earth
giai_thich: These "pre-solar" particles formed in the winds of dead stars before the Sun was born about 4.6 billion years ago. Scientists measure age by calculating the time the particles were exposed to cosmic rays while drifting in interstellar space. Murchison also contains over 70 types of amino acids, including those not found on Earth. The residents of the town of Murchison in Victoria smelled a scent similar to methyl alcohol after the meteorite fell.

cau_hoi: Why is the Ensisheim meteorite that fell in the Alsace region (present-day France) in 1492 famous?
B: It is the earliest recorded meteorite fall in Europe that still has preserved specimens
C: It is the largest meteorite in the world
giai_thich: The meteorite, weighing about 127 kg, fell on a wheat field on November 7, 1492, just weeks after Columbus landed in America. A boy witnessed it. Emperor Maximilian I considered it a sign from heaven and had it hung in a church. Today, most of the remaining 55 kg is displayed in the town of Ensisheim. It wasn't until around 1803, after a meteor shower in L'Aigle (France), that the scientific community accepted that stones could actually fall from the sky.

cau_hoi: In 1954, Ann Hodges in Alabama (USA) became the first person recorded in modern history to experience what?
D: Being struck by a meteorite that fell through her roof, hit her radio, and struck her hip while she was sleeping on the sofa
giai_thich: The meteorite, weighing about 4 kg, only caused a large bruise. Afterwards, a dispute arose between the Hodges family and the landlord over ownership of the stone. Eventually, it was donated to the Alabama Museum of Natural History. The probability of being hit by a meteorite is extremely low. In 1992, a meteorite hit a car in Peekskill (New York), surprising the owner, but later sold the damaged car for a high price to a collector.

cau_hoi: The Allende meteorite that fell in Mexico in 1969 contains small white grains that hold what record?
A: They are the first solid materials formed in the Solar System, about 4.567 billion years ago, used to determine the age of the Solar System
giai_thich: Calcium-aluminum-rich inclusions (CAIs) condensed from the hot gas cloud around the young Sun. The Allende meteorite broke into thousands of pieces, totaling about 2 tons, falling over a wide area in Chihuahua, just months before Apollo 11 brought Moon rocks back. Laboratories were preparing to analyze Moon rocks, so they studied Allende very carefully. It is one of the most studied meteorites in history.

cau_hoi: In 2024, astronomers announced evidence of a "medium-mass" black hole in the Omega Centauri star cluster. Why is this discovery important?
A: Medium-sized black holes (about 8,200 times the Sun) are very rarely found, being the "missing link" between stellar black holes and supermassive black holes
B: It is the closest black hole to Earth
C: It is the smallest black hole
D: That black hole is sucking Earth in
giai_thich: The research team used over 500 Hubble images taken over 20 years to track about 1.4 million stars and found 7 stars moving too fast, which can only be explained by a massive object at the center. Omega Centauri is likely the remnant core of a small galaxy that has been swallowed by the Milky Way. Stellar black holes weigh several tens of times the Sun, while supermassive black holes weigh millions to billions of times, so scientists have been searching for medium-sized black holes for a long time.

cau_hoi: The gravitational wave event GW190521, announced in 2020, surprised scientists for what reason?
A: The waves came from the Moon
C: Two black holes merged to create a black hole about 142 times the Sun, and an initial black hole with a mass in the "forbidden range" that theory suggests stars cannot leave behind
giai_thich: According to theory, very large stars when they explode will be completely destroyed in a "pair instability" explosion, leaving no black holes with masses around 65 – 130 times the Sun. One black hole involved in the merger weighed about 85 times the Sun, possibly itself being the result of a previous merger. The signal lasted only about 0.1 seconds. The energy released was equivalent to about 8 times the mass of the Sun completely converted into gravitational waves.

cau_hoi: "Spaghettification" is what?
D: An object falling near a black hole is stretched in the direction of the black hole and compressed sideways by tidal forces
giai_thich: The gravitational pull of a black hole on the part of the object closer to it is much stronger than on the part farther away. With a small black hole, a person would be stretched before reaching the event horizon. Interestingly, with a supermassive black hole, the difference in force at the horizon is small, so an astronaut could cross the horizon without feeling anything. When a star is torn apart near a black hole, astronomers see a flash called a "tidal disruption event," which can last for months.

cau_hoi: What are "rogue planets," and how many do scientists estimate there are in the Milky Way?
B: Planets that do not orbit any star, drifting freely in space; possibly more than the number of stars
C: Planets only found on the Moon
giai_thich: These planets may have been "kicked" out of their star systems due to gravitational interactions when the system was still young, or formed as failed small stars. They are very difficult to detect because they do not emit light; astronomers find them using "gravitational microlensing," when a planet passes in front of a distant star and briefly makes it shine. NASA's Nancy Grace Roman telescope, expected to launch around 2026 – 2027, may detect hundreds of rogue planets.

cau_hoi: The exoplanet WASP-12b is famous for what fate?
A: It is gradually spiraling closer to its host star and will be swallowed in a few million years
C: It is flying out of the Milky Way
D: It is turning into a star
giai_thich: WASP-12b is a "hot Jupiter" that orbits very close to its host star, completing a cycle in about 1.1 days. The tidal forces of the star are pulling the planet into an egg shape, and the planet is losing its atmosphere to the star. In 2019 – 2020, astronomers measured its orbital period shortening by about 29 milliseconds each year, evidence that it is gradually falling into the star. Its surface is extremely dark, reflecting very little light, as black as freshly laid asphalt.

cau_hoi: What are some lesser-known characteristics of Polaris (the North Star)?
B: It is a triple star system, the main star is a Cepheid variable star, and it is not the brightest star in the sky
D: It is the brightest star in the sky
giai_thich: Many people mistake Polaris for the brightest star, but it is actually only about the 48th brightest. Polaris is about 430 – 450 light-years away, a yellow supergiant, with brightness varying slightly over a cycle of about 4 days. Interestingly, the amplitude of its variation decreased sharply in the 20th century, then increased again. In 2024, astronomers captured images of Polaris's surface showing many blemishes. During the time of the Egyptian pyramids, the star Thuban in the Draco constellation was the North Star.

cau_hoi: The term "black hole" was popularized by physicist John Wheeler in 1967. What were these objects commonly called before that?
D: "Frozen star" or "completely collapsed star due to gravity"
giai_thich: According to accounts, during a talk, an audience member suggested the phrase "black hole" when Wheeler complained that the old name was too long, and he began to use it. The name "frozen star" comes from the observation that a collapsing star appears to slow down and "freeze" at the event horizon due to time dilation. Wheeler also coined the term "wormhole" in 1957. He was the mentor of Richard Feynman and Kip Thorne.

cau_hoi: What is the famous reason for the black hole TON 618?
A: It is the closest black hole to Earth
B: It is the first black hole to be photographed
C: It is one of the heaviest known black holes, estimated to be about 40 – 66 billion times the mass of the Sun
D: It is the smallest black hole
giai_thich: TON 618 is a bright quasar located about 10 billion light-years away, discovered in a star catalog in Mexico in 1957 (the name TON comes from the Tonantzintla Observatory). Its event horizon could be several times wider than Neptune's orbit. The mass is estimated indirectly through the speed of gas swirling around it, so there is a large margin of error. If placed in the Solar System, this black hole would swallow all the planets. The black hole at the center of the Milky Way is only about 4 million times the mass of the Sun.

cau_hoi: The James Webb Space Telescope does not orbit the Earth but operates near the Lagrange point L2. How far is this point from Earth?
giai_thich: L2 is located on the straight line between the Sun and Earth, behind the Earth, about 1.5 million km away, which is about 4 times the distance to the Moon (384,000 km). There, the Sun, Earth, and Moon always lie on the same side, so Webb's large sunshield, the size of a tennis court, can cover all three, keeping the telescope cold below −220°C to observe infrared light. 36,000 km is the altitude of a geostationary satellite.

cau_hoi: There is a new moon every month, so why is there not a solar eclipse every month?
A: The Moon's orbit is tilted about 5° relative to Earth's orbit
B: Because solar eclipses only occur in summer
C: Because the Earth rotates too quickly
D: Because the Moon is too small to cover the Sun
giai_thich: Due to the Moon's orbit being tilted about 5°, during most new moons, the Moon's shadow passes above or below the Earth. A solar eclipse only occurs when the new moon coincides with the Moon being near the intersection of the two orbital planes. This happens about twice a year, known as the "eclipse season", so there are between 2 to 5 solar eclipses somewhere on Earth each year.

cau_hoi: Why are there times when a lunar eclipse does not completely cover the Sun, leaving a bright "ring of fire" around it?
A: Clouds cover part of the Moon
B: The Sun is unusually enlarged at that time
C: The Moon is transparent at the edge
D: The Moon is farther from Earth, making it appear smaller than the Sun
giai_thich: The Moon's orbit is elliptical, with distances to Earth varying from about 356,000 km to 406,000 km. If a solar eclipse occurs when the Moon is near its farthest point (apogee), the Moon's disk appears slightly smaller than the Sun's disk, revealing a bright ring, known as an annular eclipse. At that time, it does not get completely dark and cannot be viewed directly with the naked eye.

cau_hoi: According to scientists, what strange phenomenon might be occurring deep inside Uranus and Neptune?
giai_thich: These two giant ice planets contain a lot of methane gas (composed of carbon and hydrogen). Deep inside, extreme pressure and temperature may separate carbon and compress it into diamond particles, which then sink like rain. In 2017, scientists at the SLAC laboratory (USA) used powerful lasers to shoot at a type of plastic and created tiny diamonds, supporting this hypothesis.

cau_hoi: "Roche limit" is what, and what does it help explain about Saturn's rings?
A: The farthest distance at which a planet can hold onto a moon
B: The distance within which tidal forces tear a moon apart; the rings lie within this limit
C: The temperature at which ice begins to melt
D: The maximum speed of a moon
giai_thich: In 1848, French mathematician Édouard Roche calculated that if a moon comes too close to a planet, the gravitational pull on the near side is much stronger than on the far side, tearing it apart. Most of Saturn's rings lie within this limit, so ice particles cannot coalesce into a moon. One hypothesis suggests that the rings are remnants of a moon that came too close.

cau_hoi: The unit "parsec", used by astronomers to measure distances to stars, is approximately how many light-years?
giai_thich: A parsec is short for "parallax second": the distance from which the radius of Earth's orbit appears to subtend an angle of exactly 1 arcsecond (1/3,600 degrees). One parsec is about 3.26 light-years, or about 31 trillion km. The nearest star is Proxima Centauri, about 1.3 parsecs away. Distant galaxies are often measured in megaparsecs (million parsecs).

cau_hoi: Why do astronomers use Type Ia supernovae as "standard candles" to measure distances to distant galaxies?
A: They explode when they reach nearly the same mass, so they have nearly the same intrinsic brightness
B: They are always at the same distance
D: They only appear in the Milky Way
giai_thich: Type Ia supernovae occur when a white dwarf star accretes material from a companion star until it approaches about 1.4 times the mass of the Sun and then explodes. Because they explode at the same "threshold", their intrinsic brightness is nearly the same. By comparing intrinsic brightness with the brightness we see, scientists calculate the distance. Using this method, in 1998, it was discovered that the universe is expanding at an accelerating rate.

cau_hoi: Radio astronomers map the spiral arms of the Milky Way using radiation with a wavelength of 21 cm. Where does this radiation come from?
giai_thich: Hydrogen atoms, the most abundant element in the universe, sometimes change the state of their electrons and emit radio waves of 21 cm. This phenomenon was predicted by Hendrik van de Hulst in 1944 and discovered in 1951. The 21 cm waves can penetrate thick dust clouds that obscure light, allowing us to first map the spiral shape of our own galaxy.

cau_hoi: What playful nickname do astronomers give to the galaxy that could form if the Milky Way and the Andromeda galaxy collide and merge in the distant future?
giai_thich: Andromeda is about 2.5 million light-years away and is approaching us at a speed of about 110 km/s. Previous predictions suggested that the two galaxies would collide in about 4 to 5 billion years. A 2025 study using data from the Gaia and Hubble telescopes showed that the likelihood of merging in the next 10 billion years is only about 50%. Since the stars are very far apart, almost no stars will collide.

cau_hoi: How much would a teaspoon of material taken from a neutron star weigh if brought back to Earth?
giai_thich: A neutron star is the remaining core after a supernova explosion: it is heavier than the Sun but compressed to about the size of a city, with a diameter of about 20 km. The atoms are crushed, with protons and electrons combining to form neutrons packed closely together. Therefore, just 5 ml of neutron star material weighs about several billion tons, more than the mass of a small mountain.

cau_hoi: What record-holding structure is found at the Jantar Mantar observatory in Jaipur (India), built in the early 18th century?
A: The tallest astronomical observation tower in the world
B: The largest radio antenna in the world
C: The largest stone sundial in the world
D: The largest optical telescope in the world
giai_thich: Maharaja Jai Singh II built Jantar Mantar with about 20 giant stone and brick astronomical instruments. The most prominent is the Samrat Yantra, a sundial about 27 m tall; its shadow moves about 1 mm per second, allowing for accurate time reading to about 2 seconds. He believed that larger instruments would measure more accurately. In 2010, the site was recognized by UNESCO as a World Heritage Site.

cau_hoi: Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), the most powerful explosions in the universe, were first discovered in 1967 accidentally thanks to which type of satellite?
B: The American Vela satellite used to monitor nuclear tests
giai_thich: After the nuclear test ban treaty in 1963, the U.S. launched Vela satellites to detect gamma rays from secret nuclear tests. In 1967, the satellite recorded strange gamma-ray flashes that did not resemble any bomb explosion. The results were kept secret and only published in 1973. Today we know that GRBs come from very distant galaxies, when massive stars collapse or neutron stars collide.

cau_hoi: On the night of January 1, 1801, which astronomer discovered Ceres, the first celestial body found in the asteroid belt?
giai_thich: Giuseppe Piazzi, a priest working at the Palermo Observatory (Italy), discovered a "star" moving slowly among the stars. After a few weeks, Ceres was obscured by the Sun's light and became "lost." Young mathematician Carl Friedrich Gauss invented a new method to calculate orbits, allowing Ceres to be rediscovered at the end of 1801. In 2006, Ceres was classified as a dwarf planet.

cau_hoi: On July 4, 2005, what unprecedented action did NASA's Deep Impact spacecraft take with comet Tempel 1?
A: Landed and planted a flag on the comet
B: Fired a copper projectile weighing about 370 kg into the comet to see inside
C: Pulled the comet off its orbit
D: Brought the comet back to Earth
giai_thich: The mother ship released a copper impactor, which crashed into the comet's nucleus at a speed of about 37,000 km/h, creating a bright cloud of dust and ice. Analysis of the debris revealed that the comet's nucleus is porous like powder, containing water ice, dust, and organic material. Copper was chosen for the projectile because it is less mixed with substances found in the comet, making it easier to distinguish during analysis.

cau_hoi: In 2010, what milestone did Japan's Hayabusa spacecraft achieve?
B: Flew out of the Solar System
C: Took pictures of the far side of the Moon
D: Brought samples from an asteroid back to Earth
giai_thich: Hayabusa ("falcon") reached the asteroid Itokawa in 2005. The spacecraft encountered numerous issues: a malfunctioning spinning wheel, fuel leaks, and lost communication for several weeks. Nevertheless, engineers managed to bring the spacecraft back, and on June 13, 2010, the sample capsule landed in the Australian desert with about 1,500 tiny dust particles. The next spacecraft, Hayabusa2, brought back samples from the asteroid Ryugu in 2020.

cau_hoi: The ancient Babylonians discovered that solar and lunar eclipses repeat in cycles, known as the Saros cycle. How long is this cycle approximately?
giai_thich: After about 18 years, 11 days, and 8 hours, the Sun, Earth, and Moon return to nearly the same positions, so an eclipse will "repeat" with a similar shape. Due to the extra 8 hours, the Earth has rotated an additional one-third of a turn, so the next eclipse occurs about 120° westward. Thanks to this cycle, ancient people could predict eclipses thousands of years in advance.

cau_hoi: How long can a total solar eclipse last, as viewed from a point on the ground?
giai_thich: The shadow of the Moon moves across the ground at a speed of over 1,700 km/h, so the total phase usually lasts only a few minutes; theoretically, the maximum is about 7 minutes and 32 seconds. In 1973, scientists on the supersonic Concorde flew to chase the Moon's shadow over Africa and experienced a total solar eclipse for 74 minutes, a record.

cau_hoi: In 1572, Tycho Brahe observed a "new star" shining brightly in the constellation Cassiopeia. What was the significance of this observation?
A: Proving that the Earth is the center of the universe
B: Proving that the starry sky is not immutable as ancient people believed
C: Proving that the Moon emits its own light
giai_thich: Since Aristotle's time, it was believed that the sky above the Moon was perfect and never changed. Tycho carefully measured and found that the "new star" did not shift compared to other stars, so it must be very far away, farther than the Moon. He wrote the book "De nova stella" (On the New Star), from which the term "nova" comes. Today we know it was a supernova.

cau_hoi: In 1917, why did Einstein add the "cosmological constant" to his equation, which he later referred to as his "greatest blunder"?
B: To calculate the speed of light
C: To explain why the Sun shines
D: To keep the universe static, neither contracting nor expanding
giai_thich: At that time, people believed the universe was static, so Einstein added a term to counteract the gravitational force that would pull the universe in. When Hubble discovered that the universe is expanding (1929), this constant seemed unnecessary. Ironically, since 1998, scientists have needed a "cosmological constant" to explain dark energy causing the universe to expand ever faster.

cau_hoi: "Olbers' Paradox" raises the question: if the universe is infinite and full of stars, why is the night sky dark? What is the answer from modern science?
A: The universe has a finite age and is expanding, light from distant stars has not yet reached us or has weakened
B: Because stars all go out at night
C: Because Earth blocks the light from stars
D: Because dust blocks all the light from stars
giai_thich: If stars were everywhere, every direction would have to encounter a star, and the night sky would be as bright as the Sun. Dust does not explain it, as dust absorbs light over time and would also heat up and glow. The solution is that the universe is only about 13.8 billion years old, so we only receive light from a finite region. Writer Edgar Allan Poe hinted at this in 1848.

cau_hoi: In which countries is the giant radio telescope array Square Kilometre Array (SKA), with hundreds of thousands of antennas, being built?
giai_thich: SKA is being built in remote areas with little phone and radio waves: hundreds of thousands of small tree-shaped antennas in Western Australia and hundreds of dish antennas in the Karoo region (South Africa). The project's headquarters is at Jodrell Bank (UK). When completed, SKA will be the largest radio telescope system in the world, helping to study the first stars and galaxies.

cau_hoi: Approximately how many neutrinos from the Sun pass through each square centimeter of your body every second?
giai_thich: Nuclear fusion reactions in the Sun's core produce countless neutrinos, which are extremely light particles, electrically neutral, and interact very little with matter. They pass through your body and even the Earth almost undeterred, even at night when the Sun is on the other side. In a person's lifetime, on average, only about one neutrino actually collides with an atom in their body.
